"The board were blown away by him in an extensive interview and his hunger to fix our issues and get confidence back into our talented squad is what I am most excited by."

Speaking to BBC Radio Cambridgeshire, club director Iain Crawford described the appointment as being "a calculated big swing".

He said: "We could've taken the safe option. I have no doubt that the other candidates would have got us up the table - we'd have been fine.

"I feel with most of them there was probably a ceiling. With Robbie we feel there is no ceiling.

"We felt the football club and playing style just needed a shake. As Darragh put it in one of our calls, we just need to take a big swing. That's what we've done. Robbie is a bit of a big swing."

BBC Radio Gloucestershire's Forest Green reporter Paul Furley said the most appropriate buzzword for Savage's style of football was "relentless".

That certainly tallies with how Savage wants his teams to play.

Speaking at his unveiling as Posh boss, he said he loves "entertaining, attacking football, that is my belief. I would rather win games 5-4 than 1-0."

Reflecting on Savage's 15 months at Forest Green, Furley said: "He [Savage] loves a 4-2-3-1 formation.

"In his only full season at the club, their goals scored went up from 69 to 82 compared with the previous season. Goals conceded also went up from 42 to 52.

"He revolutionised the squad at Forest Green, and only two first team regulars pre-date him. He always pointed to reducing the club's wage bill as one of the things he was tasked with and one of his major achievements."

With Peterborough second bottom of League One, and still the best part of three months away from the January transfer window, a similar approach may require patience from chairman MacAnthony and Peterborough fans alike.

"Lots was made of Robbie Savage signing a new player every time Forest Green lost a game," Furley added.

"But plenty of those were either loan signings, or players from a lower level, given opportunities to become full-time professionals.

"That inevitably has a lower immediate strike-rate of success, but is good for the health of the game.

"It also show his love of football at all levels – from Macclesfield to Forest Green, to League One where his son Charlie plays and he now manages, to the Premier League where he played and watches as a pundit."

"He was brilliant with fans," he said. "Different to anything we've seen before. He was happy to meet people, speak to people. He was quite open and honest and would front up to a good or bad result.

"He had a difficult time with transition and players coming in and out. Some fans speculated he had a hard time trusting players as many were brought in from a lower level in the National League North and South.

"Despite lots of chopping and changing, we generally played good football under him. The energy of his side was really good. Football wise, it was good to a point."

"His legacy at Macc is absolute," said Sharpley, who co-hosts the National League Lowdown podcast.

"Nobody can change what he did, with record breaking points and goals. He's part of the club's fabric. The way he left left a sour taste, but everything he did was there for all to see.

"Nobody could say he wasn't good for the club, he got eyeballs on us from the moment we were reformed. He's a big personality who would always stop to chat and shake your hand."
